newsitem.title: USA: Susan McDougal moved to new jail after ACLU protest.
newsitem.headline: Susan McDougal moved to new jail after ACLU protest.

text.p: The nation's leading civil liberties group called Wednesday for a Congressional investigation into the "inhumane" treatment of Susan McDougal as the embattled Whitewater figure won her fight for better jail conditions.

McDougal, who claims she was badly mistreated in two Los Angeles County jails because she refuses to cooperate with Whitewater prosecutor Kenneth Starr, was moved Tuesday from Los Angeles County's Twin Towers Jail to the Metropolitan Correction Centre.
The move will allow McDougal to attend state court where she is accused in an unrelated case of embezzling $150,000 from conductor Zubin Mehta.
She was ordered held in civil contempt of court by a federal judge in Little Rock, Ark., last year for refusing to testify before the Whitewater grand jury.
Sen. Robert Torricelli (D-N.J.) who in a July speech on the Senate floor called for McDougal's release, said Wednesday he was "gratified" that she had been transferred to a "more humane environment."
The American Civil Liberties Union's southern California branch called McDougal's transfer "an extremely sweet victory" but also demanded a Congressional probe into the matter.

"The abusive treatment of Ms. McDougal by Mr. Starr's office must be the subject of a Congressional investigation to ensure that, in the future, no federal prosecutor be permitted to wield authority in so brutish and inhumane a manner," Mark Rosenbaum, the ACLU of Southern California's legal director, told a news conference.
Rosenbaum said he had received a promise Wednesday morning from Assistant U.S. Attorney Rick Brooyan that McDougal would stay in the federal facility and not return to a county jail.
He said he was expecting written confirmation from Brooyan, and once it was received the ACLU would drop its lawsuit against the federal government.

The legal action, filed in U.S. District Court last week, sought McDougal's transfer from the Twin Towers jail where, it alleged, she was kept isolated from other prisoners for up to 23 hours a day and forced to wear shackles for court appearances.

The ACLU suit alleged the government was subjecting McDougal to "abusive and inhuman" treatment to force her to cooperate with Starr in his probe of President Bill Clinton. She was expected to remain in jail until the Whitewater grand jury in Little Rock is disbanded, which is expected in mid-November.
McDougal is expected to have the same prison privileges in her new home as fellow inmates, including being allowed out of her cell to mingle with other prisoners for 12 hours a day.

Starr is trying to determine if Clinton used his influence as the then-governor of Arkansas to secure McDougal and her ex-husband James McDougal an illegal government loan. Clinton and the McDougals were partners in the failed Whitewater real estate development.

A spokeswoman for Starr has denied that he had anything to do with McDougal's treatment in jail, but Rosenbaum and McDougal's brother, Bill Henley, disagreed, calling his sister a "political prisoner".
